summary: Defines SigComp, a way to compress messages from text-based signaling protocols such as SIP and RTSP. It describes the architecture and message format, and uses a Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine that can run many different decompression algorithms. It was later updated by RFC 4896.

eli5.summary: Text messages between phones can be wordy. SigComp squeezes them small before sending, and a tiny built-in computer on the other end unpacks them.

subtitle: A way to squeeze text-based signaling messages like SIP by shipping a tiny virtual machine that knows how to unpack them.

tldr.problem: Text-based signaling protocols such as SIP and RTSP produce messages that are not optimized for size, which hurts call setup on low-rate wireless links.
tldr.mechanism: SigComp sits between the application and the transport. The sender picks any compression algorithm and ships the matching decompression bytecode (or points to saved state) so the receiver's Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine (UDVM) can unpack the message.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that gives lossless, robust compression over TCP, UDP or SCTP, with strict limits on memory, CPU cycles and state to keep it safe. It was later updated by RFC 4896.

facts.label: Cycle budget
facts.value: (8 * n + 1000) * cycles_per_bit for an n-byte message

today: RFC 3320 is a Proposed Standard, and it was later updated by RFC 4896. Its companion document on extended operations is RFC 3321.

sections.title: Why Signaling Messages Need Compression
sections.content:
Many multimedia application protocols are text-based and were engineered for bandwidth-rich links, so their messages were not optimized for size. The RFC notes that typical SIP messages range from a few hundred bytes up to two thousand bytes or more. On low-rate connections in 2.5G and 3G cellular networks, that size causes real delays, and retransmissions and multi-message flows make call setup and feature invocation worse.

SigComp (Signaling Compression) offers robust, lossless compression of application messages. It is presented to applications as a layer between the application and an underlying transport. The service is that of the transport plus compression, and it works over TCP, UDP and SCTP. The RFC names SIP and RTSP as example application protocols.

Decompression is done by a Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine (UDVM), a virtual machine designed only for running decompression algorithms. Because the compressor can upload the bytecode for whichever algorithm it chose, it is not limited to a short list of pre-negotiated algorithms. The abstract says the UDVM can be configured to understand the output of well-known compressors such as DEFLATE.
sections.eli5: Long, wordy messages are slow to send on a slow connection. SigComp shrinks them first, like folding a big letter small so it fits in a tiny envelope.

sections.title: The SigComp Architecture
sections.content:
Compression and decompression happen at two communicating endpoints. Inside the SigComp layer of one endpoint there are five kinds of part:

  • A compressor dispatcher that takes an application message plus a compartment identifier and hands it to the right compressor.
  • A decompressor dispatcher that receives SigComp messages, runs a UDVM and passes the result to the application.
  • One or more compressors, chosen per compartment, each free to use its own algorithm (for example DEFLATE).
  • The UDVM. A separate instance is invoked for every message, because SigComp can run over an unsecured transport.
  • The state handler, which stores and retrieves state that lives between messages. New state can only be created with the permission of the application.

The choice to use SigComp is made independently in each direction, and the two directions need not use the same algorithm. From a multi-hop application point of view, SigComp is applied per hop.

A compartment is an application-specific grouping of messages related to a peer endpoint, such as a session, dialog or connection. The application decides when one is created or closed, and must give distinct remote endpoints distinct compartments. All SigComp messages start with a prefix whose five most-significant bits of the first byte are set to one. That pattern does not occur in UTF-8 text, so SigComp and uncompressed messages can share a port.

On a stream-based transport, messages are delimited by record marking: the byte 0xFF is special. 0xFF 00 stands for one literal 0xFF, 0xFF 01 to 0xFF 7F quote the next 1 to 127 bytes, and 0xFF FF ends a SigComp message. The dispatcher must never concatenate two SigComp messages into one UDVM run.

When the application gets a decompressed message, it may return a compartment identifier. That grants permission to save state and to trust the feedback data. If it fails to authenticate the message, it reports "no valid compartment" and no state is created.
sections.eli5: Think of two post offices that each have a packer and an unpacker. The packer picks how to fold the letter, and the unpacker follows folding instructions that came in the envelope.

sections.title: Endpoint Parameters and Limits
sections.content:
Endpoints differ in memory and processing power, so SigComp defines parameters that tell a compressor what the receiver can handle: decompression_memory_size, state_memory_size, cycles_per_bit, SigComp_version and the set of locally available state items. Every receiving endpoint MUST offer a decompression_memory_size of at least 2048 bytes and a minimum of 16 cycles_per_bit. Endpoints MAY offer more and can advertise it through the feedback mechanism.

The state_memory_size is offered per compartment and is 0 for a stateless endpoint. The values come from small fixed sets so they fit in a few bits: cycles_per_bit uses 2 bits (16, 32, 64 or 128), and the two memory sizes use 3 bits each. The decompression memory encoding is the same as for state memory, except that the pattern 000 cannot be used.

The basic version of SigComp is Version 0x01. Upgraded versions must stay backwards compatible, for example by adding UDVM instructions or by giving values to reserved memory addresses. IANA created a 1-byte namespace for SigComp_version, and new values need a Standards Action.

Locally available state items are pieces of data an endpoint offers without a remote endpoint uploading them, such as well-known decompression algorithms or a dictionary of common phrases. The RFC gives the example of a SIP phrase dictionary being made mandatory for SigComp used with SIP.
sections.eli5: Some phones are strong and some are small. Before sending, you check how big a backpack the other side has, so you do not hand over more than it can carry.

sections.title: State Handling and Feedback
sections.content:
Using a fresh UDVM per message means a damaged or forged message cannot break later ones. But compression is much better when a message can refer to earlier ones, so SigComp allows state items that later messages can load. Creation and access are designed to resist tampering. State is only created after a message has been fully decompressed and the application has returned a compartment identifier.

Access is protected by a state identifier, a 20-byte hash of the state item. A sender may supply as few as 6 bytes of it, but each state item has a minimum_access_length that stops brute-force guessing. State is not deleted when accessed, so even if an attacker reads it, later valid messages still decompress.

The state handler tracks memory per compartment. Each item costs state_length + 64 bytes against the compartment's state_memory_size. One UDVM run can make up to four state creation requests and four state free requests. When space runs out, items with the lowest state_retention_priority are freed first, with ties going to the oldest. A priority of 65535 is reserved for locally available state, which is freed first.

An optional feedback exchange works when each side has a matching compartment for the other. A compressor piggybacks a feedback request on a message. The remote side returns the data, which can include its capabilities, on a message going the other way. The compressor SHOULD return any requested feedback in its next SigComp message. The sender is responsible for feedback arriving over an unreliable transport, and the receiver uses the last value it received.
sections.eli5: It is like a shared notebook. After you have written a long page once, later you just say "see page 5". The page code is hard to guess, so strangers cannot peek.

sections.title: The SigComp Message Format
sections.content:
A SigComp message starts with the five one-bits, then a T bit and a 2-bit len field. The T bit says whether a returned feedback item follows. That item is 1 to 128 bytes in total, with a feedback field of 0 to 127 bytes.

The len field chooses between two forms. If it is non-zero, the message carries a partial state identifier of 6, 9 or 12 bytes, which names a saved state item to load. The state's data is copied into UDVM memory and execution starts at that item's state_instruction address. A decompression failure occurs if zero or several items match, or if the partial identifier is shorter than the item's minimum_access_length.

If len is 0, the bytecode is uploaded in the message. A 12-bit code_len field gives its size (0 to 4095 bytes), and a 4-bit destination field picks the memory address it is copied to. The value 0000 is reserved and causes decompression failure in Version 0x01. The rest of the message is the compressed data, which the UDVM pulls in only when an instruction asks for it. That is why it can start decompressing before the whole message has arrived.

The first 32 bytes of UDVM memory are filled with "useful values": memory size, cycles_per_bit, the SigComp version, and the lengths for any accessed state. All other memory is zero.
sections.eli5: Each message starts with a label saying either "use the instructions you saved earlier, here is the code" or "here are the instructions, folded inside". The packed data comes after.

sections.title: How the UDVM Runs
sections.content:
The UDVM is a small virtual machine, a bit like the Java Virtual Machine but built only for decompression. The RFC says typical decompression bytecode is small, often under 100 bytes. Its registers are 2-byte words in memory: byte_copy_left, byte_copy_right, input_bit_order and stack_location, at addresses 64 to 71. The input_bit_order flags let it match the bit orders of algorithms such as DEFLATE. A stack of 2-byte words supports CALL, RETURN, PUSH and POP.

The machine understands 36 instructions. They cover bit and arithmetic operations, sorting, SHA-1, loading and copying memory, jumps and switches, a CRC check, input of bytes, bits or Huffman codes, state access, creation and freeing, OUTPUT and END-MESSAGE. Operands use variable-length encoding so that common values take fewer bytes, and address operands make the code position-independent.

To stop a message from consuming too much CPU, each run has a cycle budget. For an n-byte message the maximum is (8 * n + 1000) * cycles_per_bit, and each instruction costs at least one cycle. Decompression failure happens for things like an invalid header, a message larger than decompression_memory_size, running out of cycles, bad memory access, an unknown instruction, or a DECOMPRESSION-FAILURE instruction triggered by bytecode, for example when a CRC check fails. The dispatcher SHOULD then discard the message. Total output may not exceed 65536 bytes.

The END-MESSAGE instruction finishes a run. It reports the end to the application, passes up to four state creation requests and four state free requests to the state handler, and can include feedback data. The compressor is expected to include some integrity check, and the UDVM offers CRC and SHA-1 instructions for that.
sections.eli5: The tiny computer only knows 36 simple moves, like copy, add and jump. That is enough for the sender to teach it any unpacking recipe. It also has a timer so a tricky recipe cannot run forever.

sections.title: Security Goals and Risks
sections.content:
The stated security goal is to add no risks beyond those of the application protocol: do not worsen existing security, do not create new issues, and do not hinder application security. SigComp does not try to add security of its own, and it assumes appropriate integrity protection below or above the SigComp layer.

For confidentiality, state is reached only by supplying part of a hash of the state, so the sender must already know its content. At least 48 bits of the hash are needed, and a compressor can require more with minimum_access_length. Endpoints should treat state identifiers as carefully as the state itself. For integrity, state cannot be changed by a sender who cannot send messages the application assigns to the same compartment, and faking state would need a hash collision.

For availability, SigComp is not an easy reflection amplifier because it produces one decompressed message per incoming message. It can still turn small packets into larger ones, so the application MUST limit the number of packets reflected to a target. Excess state needs the application's consent. The cycle limit bounds damage from looping code, and the UDVM cycles and memory are capped per message. The RFC warns that the "continuous mode" needs lower-level denial-of-service protection such as TLS, because an attacker could otherwise create any number of active UDVMs.
sections.eli5: The rules make sure the shrinking trick cannot be used to sneak in trouble. The helper only follows allowed steps, runs on a timer and keeps its notebook locked with hard-to-guess codes.
